edges.label: The topic 'Applications (coupon collector, sieve of Eratosthenes)' introduces boolean_flag_array.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: using a value (a card number) as a position is not how everyday checklists work; people search a list to see whether they have seen something. Java rule: found[val] is the flag stored at index val, so one indexed read answers 'seen val?'.
[1] misconception (M) -> OffByOneBound: wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: To use the value N itself as an index, the array must have length N+1 (new boolean[N+1]), and loops over values 2..N use i <= N.
[2] misconception (M) -> NewArrayHoldsGarbage: wrong rule: The slots of a new boolean[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned. Right rule: new boolean[n] starts every flag at false.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> OffByOneBound: Points to LT: for each new value, test found[val] and, only if it is false, count it and set the flag. Inconsistent application: the flag is set before the test on some passes, so a new value is counted as already seen. (here mixing in: "< vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable")

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: a boolean array indexed by value, in which flag[v] records whether v has been seen or has a property.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: create boolean[] flags = new boolean[N] (all false); mark v with flags[v] = true; test with if (!flags[v]). Values must lie in 0..N-1.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing (CouponCollector): generate val, increment cardcnt, test found[val], and if it is false increment valcnt and set found[val] = true; repeat while valcnt < N.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: the count derived from the flags, e.g. CouponCollector prints the number of cards drawn, and PrimeSieve 25 prints 9; at the end of the collector found[] is all true.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one step sets at most one flag from false to true and never back, so each element is a one-way flag.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): new boolean[n] starts every flag at false, which CouponCollector relies on; PrimeSieve needs true and so sets it with a loop.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): The sieve traverses isPrime[] to set every flag to true and later traverses it again to count the flags still true.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: set membership by direct indexing. Each element is a one-way flag (Sajaniemi), and the array lets data index into the array, turning 'have I seen v?' into one step.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> OffByOneBound: Conservation: in CouponCollector, valcnt always equals the number of true entries in found[]. Enlarging the value range requires enlarging the array (N+1 when N itself is an index).
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: use a flag array when the values are small non-negative integers (card values, numbers up to N) and memory for N flags is affordable. Do not use one for huge, negative or non-integer keys.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Values used as indices must lie in 0..length-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: new boolean[N] used with value N as an index (the sieve needs N+1), or a negative value (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A start value other than false must be set explicitly. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: PrimeSieve without its initial isPrime[i] = true loop: no number is ever prime, so it prints 0
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Test the flag before setting it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: found[val] = true written before if (!found[val]), so valcnt never increases and the loop never ends
